$comment: Rules about financial arithmetic and how figures are expressed. Standards 10, 11, 12, and 28. Only the Standard 11 rules exist at this milestone; the rest land with their standards, because a rule backlinking to a standard nobody has written points at nothing — scripts/inventory.mjs now refuses that.
$admissionTest: Every rule here passed all five questions (ADR 0005): can it be applicable, can evidence be gathered, can its state be evaluated, can its violation be explained, can remediation change the result? Standard 11's other requirements — whether an inflation assumption is reasonable, whether a cross-period comparison's basis is the right one — fail question three and stay in the standard's prose, disclosed in its Implementation section.

rules.title: Every stated return is labelled nominal or real
rules.description: Each return, growth rate, or projected monetary figure in the analysis states whether it is expressed in nominal terms or in real, inflation-adjusted terms.
rules.rationale: An unlabelled return is ambiguous by exactly the inflation rate, and the reader has no way to recover which was meant. Over a long horizon the two differ by most of the answer.
rules.remediation: Label each figure at the point it is stated. A single global note does not disambiguate a document that mixes both, which most realistic analyses do.
rules.$assuranceNote: A lexical check. It establishes that a label is PRESENT near a figure — never that the label is CORRECT. A nominal figure labelled 'real' passes this check, and no scan available to this repository can tell the difference. Reporting a clean run as 'nominal and real are not confused here' would be exactly the false green this framework exists to prevent.

rules.title: Long-horizon projections lead with real terms
rules.description: Where the projection horizon exceeds ten years, the analysis presents its primary figures in today's purchasing power, with nominal figures secondary.
rules.rationale: A nominal figure at a thirty-year horizon reads as a far better outcome than it is, and reads that way most strongly to the audience least equipped to notice.
rules.remediation: Convert the headline figures to today's money and state the inflation assumption used. Keep the nominal figures; make them secondary.
rules.$assuranceNote: Recommended rather than required because legitimate exceptions exist: a fixed nominal liability such as a mortgage balance genuinely is a nominal quantity, and converting it obscures more than it clarifies. The checker cannot distinguish that case from an oversight, which is precisely why this warns rather than fails.
